query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The simple solid‐solution state in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has lower hardness and yield strength because it lacks significant local chemical ordering (LCO) or nanoscale ordered precipitates (e.g. B2‐like regions) that act as obstacles for dislocation motion. In contrast, such LCO, when developed (for example, via controlled annealing), increases resistance to slip (thereby enhancing strength and hardness) at the expense of some ductility. This difference in dislocation barrier efficiency explains why the alloy is very plastic and machinable yet exhibits relatively low hardness and strength in its as‐quenched state.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced as a single-phase random solid solution (water-quenched or rapidly cooled) showing favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment (e.g., homogenization followed by slow cooling or annealing) designed to promote local chemical ordering (LCO) or the formation of nanoscale ordered regions (e.g., B2-like precipitates) within the matrix.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing conducted at room temperature (≈25 °C) and at elevated temperature (up to 600 °C) under quasi-static tensile and compression loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence (or absence) of local chemical order in the alloy microstructure that acts as a barrier to dislocation glide.
generation.mechanism: In the disordered (random solid solution) state, dislocations can glide with little resistance, leading to lower yield strength and hardness but high ductility. By inducing LCO, atomic-scale ordering increases lattice distortions and creates more effective obstacles to dislocation motion, thereby increasing the yield stress and hardness. However, the increased barriers also reduce plastic strain capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the thermally treated (LCO-enhanced) CoCrFeNiTi alloy will exhibit a higher hardness and yield strength and reduced plastic strain during compressive and tensile tests both at room temperature and at 600 °C.
generation.baseline: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its as-quenched, random solid-solution state, which shows relatively low hardness and strength but favorable ductility/machinability.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in its simple solid-solution state versus its LCO-enhanced state under quasi-static loading at 25 °C and up to 600 °C. It does not address variations induced by adding extra alloying elements or extreme processing conditions that lead to multiphase microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative shifts in strength and hardness due to LCO are not precisely known and may vary with the details of the thermal treatment. Additionally, the temperature dependence of LCO effects might introduce variations not fully predictable without direct experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one processed by rapid quenching to maintain a random solid solution, and a second subjected to a controlled annealing/slow-cooling treatment to promote LCO. Confirm the presence or absence of LCO using microstructural tools such as TEM, XRD, and atom probe tomography (APT). Then, carry out quasi-static tensile and compressive tests at 25 °C and 600 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled annealing treatment does not lead to a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength (with a corresponding decrease in plastic strain) compared to the as-quenched samples, then the hypothesis—that the presence of LCO controls the balance of deformation, hardness, and strength—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, local chemical order (LCO), as a strategy for strengthening MEAs and HEAs, has received widespread attention (). According to the different dimensions, LCO can be classified as short-range order (SRO; below 1 nm) and medium-range order (MRO, 1 to 5 nm) and both play a major role in influencing micromechanical behaviors and elevating strength/hardness of alloys (). Inspired by this, here, we develop a Fe49Mn30Co10Cr10N1 (at %) HEA with ultrahigh strength and satisfactory ductility at the ambient-to-cryogenic temperature range, by combining the concept of interstitial-driven LCO strengthening and phase metastability. The material shows a heterostructure with an inhomogeneous distribution of chemical compositions due to the formation of multiscaled LCO structures and a nonuniform distribution of grain sizes caused by partial recrystallization. A novel deformation mechanism involving the development of LCO during plastic deformation proves to be very effective in obtaining ultrastrong and ductile FCC materials, as LCO domains with the enlarged dimensions strengthen the alloy and change the slip mode of dislocations from planar to wavy slips. Tests in the polycrystalline single-phase state have shown that CrMnFeCoNi exhibits certain noteworthy mechanical properties, including significant temperature dependence of yield stress coupled with moderate strain-rate sensitivity at low homologous temperatures, and positive correlation between strength and ductility, and strength and toughness at cryogenic temperatures. These features cannot be easily modeled in terms of the behavior of simple FCC solid solutions given that there are no “solvent” or “solute” atoms in equiatomic alloys. Although, in principle, the temperature dependence of yield stress (increasing strength with decreasing temperature) implies some sort of thermally activated process of yielding, the fundamentals of solid-solution hardening and plastic deformation have not yet been fully characterized or quantified. This is due in part to the difficulty of obtaining large single crystals of the HEA. Only very recently has a paper been published on the growth and compression testing of a bulk single crystal of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA; however, just one loading axis [51] was tested and the authors did not perform any dislocation analysis.

In summary, the study reveals that the maximum strength and critical grain size can be manipulated by tuning the degree of chemical SRO, signifying the nontrivial role of local chemical ordering on the ultimate strength of MPEAs. As the salient feature of MPEAs, the presence of SRO considerably affects deformation microstructure and local plastic strain, originating from its effects on SF energy increase and diffuse antiphase boundary development. As a result, the volume fracture of deformation hcp atoms is decreased to compensate the increased SF energy, and plastic strain is more localized to embrace slip-mediated SRO destruction and glide plane softening. The crystal orientation of constituent grains plays a vital role in deformation mechanisms, microstructure evolution, and dislocation patterning, which collectively affect the mechanical behavior of individual grains and, hence, system-level performance.
